summary: Gives suggestions and guidance for designing the tables and algorithms a host needs to keep track of names, addresses, ports and routes inside a TCP/IP implementation. It is advice, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives advice on how a TCP/IP host can keep track of computer names, network addresses, service ports, and routes. Its central design suggestion is to keep lookup behind replaceable interfaces so implementations can adapt as the network grows.

questions: tcp ip names addresses ports routes
why are ports not part of ip
how does a host find a gateway
how does ip decide where to send a datagram
subtitle: Design advice for a TCP/IP host's name, address, port, and route tables.

tldr.problem: A TCP/IP host must translate human-readable names and service names into addresses, ports, and paths for sending packets.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends small, updateable caches and software interfaces that let a host replace static tables with distributed lookup services.
tldr.outcome: It is design guidance for host implementations, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 814 is advice for designing TCP/IP host tables and algorithms. It does not define a protocol or require implementations to use a particular design.

sections.title: Four Kinds of Network Information
sections.content:
The memo distinguishes names for networks, hosts, and services from the values used to deliver packets. A host name maps to an Internet address; a service name maps to a port identifier; an address maps to a route, the sequence of steps a packet follows.

Because the network can grow and names can change, the memo argues that a host should not depend on one permanently complete table of every name and route.
sections.plainLanguage: A name identifies a destination for people; an address and route tell the network where to send data. A service port helps deliver the data to the right program on the destination host.

sections.title: Name Lookup and Caches
sections.content:
The memo describes a move from distributing one complete name table to using name servers that maintain names for their own networks. A host can keep a cache of names it recently used and ask an appropriate name server when a name is missing.

It recommends making the name table available through a subroutine interface rather than letting unrelated parts of the implementation access it directly. That separation makes it easier to replace a local table with calls to remote name servers.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can remember names it has recently looked up and ask a name server for others. Keeping lookup behind one software interface makes that change easier.

sections.title: Choosing a Route to a Network
sections.content:
For an outgoing datagram, IP determines whether the destination is on the directly connected network. If it is not, the host sends the packet to a gateway for forwarding.

The memo recommends keeping routing information for destinations in a local table. If no suitable gateway is known, a host can try an accessible gateway and update its table when an ICMP redirect reports a better one. It also discusses source-route options, which let a sender specify a route through gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: The host sends a packet directly when the destination is on its local network. Otherwise, it chooses a gateway and can update its choice when it learns of a better route.

sections.title: Ports Identify Programs
sections.content:
An IP address gets a datagram to a host, but the transport protocol must deliver it to the intended process or connection. The memo calls the higher-level identifier a port and explains why it belongs outside the IP layer.

Keeping port dispatch in higher-level protocols avoids forcing all protocols to use the same port size or service assignment rules. It also means gateways do not need to understand application ports in order to forward IP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP address selects a host; a port selects a program or connection on that host. The memo recommends keeping those jobs separate so IP gateways can forward packets without knowing about programs.
